source_text: Εἷς δέ, ὀνόματι Κόϊντος, Φρύξ προσφάτως ἐληλυθὼς ἀπὸ τῆς Φρυγίας, ἰδὼν τὰ θηρία ἐδειλίασεν. οὗτος δὲ ἦν ὁ παραβιασάμενος ἑαυτόν τε καί τινας προσελθεῖν ἑκόντας. τοῦτον ὁ ἀνθύπατος πολλὰ ἐκλιπαρήσας ἔπεισεν ὀμόσαι καὶ ἐπιθῦσαι. διὰ τοῦτο οὖν, ἀδελφοί, οὐκ ἐπαινοῦμεν τοὺς προδιδόντας ἑαυτούς, ἐπειδὴ οὐχ οὕτως διδάσκει τὸ εὐαγγέλιον.
thought_title: Quintus's fear and the lesson against self-surrender
orientation: The church of Smyrna is reporting the martyrdoms, and after describing Germanicus's courage it now tells of Quintus, a Phrygian who had forced himself and others to come forward voluntarily but then shrank back.
pass_a_gloss: But one, by name Quintus, a Phrygian recently arrived from Phrygia, when he saw the wild beasts, he lost courage. But this man was the one who had compelled himself and certain others to come forward willingly. This man the proconsul, after much pleading, persuaded to swear by Caesar's fortune and to offer sacrifice. For this reason, therefore, brothers, we do not praise those who hand themselves over, since the gospel does not teach in this way.

choices.why: The verb denotes becoming cowardly or afraid; 'lost courage' captures the moment of fear at seeing the beasts without over-dramatizing.

choices.term: παραβιασάμενος ἑαυτόν τε καί τινας προσελθεῖν ἑκόντας
choices.english: had forced himself and certain others to come forward voluntarily
choices.why: The paradox of forcing oneself to act voluntarily is deliberate in the Greek; keeping both 'forced' and 'voluntarily' preserves the irony the author intends.
rejected: had compelled himself and some others to surrender themselves
had urged himself and others to volunteer

choices.why: The participle conveys repeated, earnest entreaty by the proconsul; 'after much pleading' keeps the proconsul as the active persuader.
The verb means to give oneself up or betray oneself; 'hand themselves over' is literal and preserves the negative connotation of self-surrender.

choices.english: the gospel does not teach in this way
choices.why: The negation is emphatic and the present tense indicates the gospel's ongoing teaching; the word order keeps the gospel as subject.
rejected: the gospel does not teach thus
this is not what the gospel teaches

pass_b_english: But one man, named Quintus, was a Phrygian who had recently come from Phrygia. When he saw the wild beasts, he lost his courage. This was the very man who had forced himself and certain others to come forward of their own accord. The proconsul pleaded with him at length and persuaded him to swear the oath and offer sacrifice. For this reason, then, brothers and sisters, we do not praise those who hand themselves over, because the gospel does not teach this.
